review.summary: Reviewed record.rs, identity.rs, signer.rs, store.rs and directory.rs through the concurrency, panics and unwraps lens. Remote-input paths into record verification are guarded: the length and identity-count checks run before indexing at record.rs:177, the expiry arithmetic saturates, and the size cap runs before decoding. The store's lock is never held across an await and make_room cannot panic. One concrete defect is a detached pruner task that is not cancelled when the serve future is dropped. One low-confidence hypothesis concerns CPU-bound verification on the async runtime.

findings.title: Pruner task leaks when serve_with_policy future is dropped
findings.prerequisites: The caller drops the future returned by serve or serve_with_policy, which the doc comment at line 56 says is how the server is stopped. This is an ordinary runtime condition, not remote input.
findings.impact: The abort at line 84 runs only after axum::serve returns normally. If the future is dropped mid-serve, the spawned pruner keeps running forever, holding an Arc to the store and calling prune every minute. A process that starts and stops the directory repeatedly accumulates such tasks.
findings.evidence: let pruner = { let store = store.clone(); tokio::spawn(async move { let mut tick = tokio::time::interval(Duration::from_secs(60)); loop { tick.tick().await; store.prune(); } }) }; let res = axum::serve(listener, router_with_policy(store, policy)).await; pruner.abort(); res
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap the JoinHandle in a guard struct whose Drop impl calls abort, or run the pruner inside the same future with tokio::select! so it is cancelled with the server.
findings.validation_needed: Demonstrated code defect by reading. Confirm with a test that drops the serve future and checks that the pruner task is finished or that the store's Arc strong count returns to 1.

findings.title: Record verification runs CPU-bound signature recovery on the async runtime
findings.prerequisites: An anonymous client sends many PUT requests, each a maximum-size record with up to 16 identities and one endpoint signature, which is about 17 signature checks per request (see the known limit on signature cost).
findings.impact: VerifiedRecord::verify is synchronous and runs directly in the axum handler without spawn_blocking. Enough concurrent PUTs could occupy all tokio worker threads and delay other tasks, including the pruner and health checks. This is hypothesis-level: the per-request cost has not been measured here, and the known limit already covers flood cost.
findings.evidence: async fn put_record(State(dir): State<Dir>, body: Bytes) -> Response { let rec = match VerifiedRecord::verify(&body) { Ok(rec) => rec, ...
findings.suggested_fix: Run verification with tokio::task::spawn_blocking, or bound concurrent verifications with a semaphore, and measure per-PUT latency under load.
findings.validation_needed: Benchmark PUT throughput with 16-identity records and check whether health latency rises under concurrent load on a small worker pool.

limitations: The deployment's runtime flavour, worker count, and any proxy or concurrency limits in front of the directory are not in the supplied source.
The CLI startup code and the callers of serve, store and sign_record are not supplied, so panic reachability from them and shutdown ordering could not be checked.
The iroh and axum internals (for example postcard's allocation limits and axum's handling of connection errors) are not in the supplied source and were assumed to behave as documented.

Clippy lint hits such as expect_used in signer.rs and the store's expect('poisoned') calls were judged unreachable from remote input, because no panic can occur while those locks are held; this was not verified by test.
Tests were read but not run; the concurrency behaviour of the store under parallel inserts was not exercised.
